newsitem.title: GERMANY: EU's de Silguy sees timely start to EMU.
newsitem.headline: EU's de Silguy sees timely start to EMU.

text.p: EU Monetary Affairs Commissioner Yves-Thibault de Silguy said on Wednesday he was certain European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) would start on January 1, 1999 with no softening of the convergence criteria.
"In my view there is not even the trace of a doubt" that January 1, 1999 will be the start date, he told a public session of the German parliamentary committee on European Affairs.
De Silguy said this was affirmed by European finance ministers at their regular meetings in Florence, Madrid and Dublin.

A delay in the start date would have negative political as well as economic consequences, as it would require a renegotiation of the Maastricht Treaty, which has been ratified by 15 countries, de Silguy said.
"Europe would lose credibility vis-a-vis its citizens and the rest of the world," he said. "The January 1999 start date is just as important as the strict application of the criteria," he said.
"A delay would be destructive, and would act counter to our aims" by putting upward pressure on interest rates and inflation, he said.
Europe also has no choice but to apply the convergence criteria of the Maastricht Treaty strictly, he added. "That is the only way to make the euro strong and stable."
De Silguy added he believed EMU would start with a meaningful number of participants, including Germany.

Finance Minister Theo Waigel, who presented his convergence report to his European counterparts on Monday, received their acknowledgment that German unification had put special strains on its debt level.
That did not mean the debt rule would be bent for Germany, de Silguy said, but he believed Germany would meet the targets on the strength of its own efforts.

All countries that fulfil the criteria will be able to participate in the euro, and the judgment of the starting participants, to be made in one year, will be made solely on the basis of economic, not geographic considerations, he said.

The European Commission will make the decision next spring on the basis of 1997 economic data, but it will also review the nations' budget plans for 1998 to ensure that stability is long-lasting. ((-- Terence Gallagher, Bonn newsroom, 49-228-2609750))
